opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest shift for me was starting to think of tool design the way you'd think about designing an interface for a human. We spend a ton of time on prompts, but people often throw together a tool definition in five minutes and never look at it again. I'd say you should put at least as much effort into the agent-computer interface as you would into a good human-computer interface.

In practice, the first thing I do is put myself in the model's shoes. I read the tool description and ask: if I were a smart new hire seeing this for the first time, with no other context, would I know exactly how to use it? Usually the answer is no. There are implicit assumptions, edge cases nobody wrote down, and parameter names that only make sense if you wrote the code. So you write it like a really good docstring: example usage, what the edge cases are, how this tool differs from the similar one next to it.

The second thing is to just run it a lot and watch what the model does. Look at the transcripts. You'll see the model make the same kind of mistake over and over, and that's usually a sign the tool is the problem, not the model. Then you change the tool so the mistake is harder to make. We called this poka-yoke, like mistake-proofing in manufacturing.

A concrete example from our SWE-bench work: the model would use relative file paths, then change directories, and the paths would break. We could have added instructions saying "be careful with relative paths," but it was much more robust to require absolute paths everywhere. Once we did that, the whole class of errors disappeared.

Format matters too. Some formats are much easier for a model to produce than others. Writing a diff means knowing how many lines changed in the hunk header before you've written the new code, which is unnatural. Making the model escape a bunch of code inside JSON adds overhead too. So you want formats that resemble what the model has seen a lot of naturally on the internet, and that give it room to think before committing to something.

So my short answer: treat the tools as a first-class part of the system, write them for a reader with no context, test empirically, and when you see repeated errors, redesign the tool instead of piling more instructions into the prompt.

r001.rationale: It recommends running the tool, reviewing transcripts for repeated mistakes, and using those patterns to revise the tool.

r002.rationale: It advocates redesigning tools to make repeated errors harder, illustrated by requiring absolute paths to prevent path failures.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing I always come back to is that you have to treat tool design like product design, except your user is the model. And the best way to understand your user is to actually watch them struggle. So a huge part of my process is just reading transcripts. Lots of them. I'll sit down and go through hundreds of agent trajectories and look for the places where the model gets confused, calls the wrong tool, passes the wrong argument, or just does something weird and roundabout when there should have been an obvious path.

And nine times out of ten, when the model does something dumb, it's not really the model's fault. It's that the tool description was ambiguous, or two tools overlap in a way that's unclear, or the output format buried the one piece of information the model actually needed under a wall of noise. If a smart new engineer joined your team and you handed them that same tool with that same documentation, they'd probably make the same mistake. So that's the test I use: would a human be confused by this? If yes, fix the tool, not the prompt.

The other thing I'd say is to keep the tool surface small and the semantics crisp. There's a temptation to give the model a tool for everything, and it actually makes things worse, because now the model has to spend reasoning on which of twelve similar things to call. I'd much rather have a few well-shaped tools with really clear boundaries and really good error messages. Error messages are underrated, by the way. When a call fails, the error should tell the model what to do next, not just that something went wrong.

And then you have to actually measure it. Build evals where the task requires the tool, run the before and after, and don't trust your intuition about whether a change helped. I've been surprised plenty of times by changes I was sure would help that did nothing, and little wording tweaks that moved the number a lot. So it's this loop: read transcripts, form a hypothesis, change the tool, run the eval, repeat. It's not glamorous, but that loop is where most of the improvement comes from.

r001.rationale: It recommends reading many agent transcripts and trajectories to find confusion and tool-use mistakes, then using those observations to revise the tools.

r002.rationale: It advocates clear tool descriptions, boundaries, outputs, and actionable error messages to prevent model usage errors.

astra-6.text:
I think of it a lot like designing an API for another engineer. You want the tools to be easy to understand, and you want it to be clear when to use each one and what to expect back.

The most useful thing is to look at the model actually using them. Where does it get confused? Is it passing the wrong arguments? Is it getting a huge amount of output and struggling to find the relevant information? Those are often problems you can fix in the tool interface instead of adding more instructions to the prompt.

Then you make a change and test it on real tasks. Sometimes a better error message or a simpler return format makes a bigger difference than giving the model another tool.

r001.rationale: It recommends examining the model’s tool use to find confusion and wrong arguments, but does not mention using transcripts of those attempts.

r002.rationale: It recommends making tools clear about how and when to use them, and adjusting the interface to address errors such as wrong arguments.

sol-6.1.text: I think of it as designing an interface for the model. You want to give it tools that are easy to understand, with clear inputs and useful outputs. Then you look at actual attempts to use them: Where does the model get confused? Is it choosing the wrong tool, passing the wrong arguments, or struggling to interpret the result? Sometimes the biggest improvement comes from changing the tool description or making an error message actionable. The key is to iterate on the whole interaction, rather than assuming every failure needs a smarter model.

r001.rationale: It recommends examining actual tool-use attempts to find problems, but does not clearly say to use transcripts of those attempts to guide revisions.

r002.rationale: It advocates clear inputs, useful outputs, and actionable error messages to reduce confusion and mistakes in tool use.
